title: How Buffett ran his partnership 1957-61: undervalued generals, work-outs, control, and beating the Dow
summary: Buffett's early partnership letters lay out his method: buy undervalued securities with a margin of safety, split capital among generals, work-outs and control situations, and judge results against the Dow over years, not months. They show his temperament toward bull markets, the Sanborn Map and Dempster control cases, and his view of true conservatism.

principles.text: Judge performance over years against a stated yardstick; one year is far too short to mean anything.
principles.quote: My own thinking is much more geared to five year performance, preferably with tests of relative results in both strong and weak markets.

principles.text: A good investment record is mostly about doing better in down markets, not matching the Dow in up ones.
principles.quote: I would consider a year in which we declined 15% and the Average 30% to be much superior to a year when both we and the Average advanced 20%.

principles.text: Buy undervalued generals with a big excess of value over price; this gives a margin of safety and diversification.
principles.quote: This individual margin of safety, coupled with a diversity of commitments creates a most attractive package of safety and appreciation potential.

principles.text: True conservatism comes from correct facts and reasoning, not from agreement with the crowd or important people.
principles.quote: You will be right, over the course of many transactions, if your hypotheses are correct, your facts are correct, and your reasoning is correct. True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason.

principles.text: Do not forecast the market; focus on finding undervalued securities, and be wary when the public believes profits from stocks are inevitable.
principles.quote: I make no attempt to forecast the general market - my efforts are devoted to finding undervalued securities.

principles.text: While accumulating a position, you want the stock to stay dull or fall; patience in buying maximizes long-term profit.
principles.quote: Obviously during any acquisition period, our primary interest is to have the stock do nothing or decline rather than advance.
